procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated December 13, 14, 1967 of the Bombay High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 380 of 1966.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Bombay High Court heard Criminal Appeal No. 380 of 1966, and delivered a judgment and order on December 13 and 14, 1967. The outcome of the appeal is not explicitly stated, but it can be inferred that the High Court upheld the conviction of the appellant (Accused No. 4) to some extent, as he is appealing that decision to the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court granted special leave to appeal only to Accused No. 4. The Supreme Court initially declined special leave against the conviction of the other three co-accused, making their convictions final. The Supreme Court, deviating from its usual practice under Article 136 of the Constitution, examined the evidence because it was represented that the evidence did not support the High Court's conclusion and that grave injustice had been caused.

decision.conviction_status: The conviction for the charges under s. 302 read with s. 109 I.P.C. and of conspiracy is upheld. The conviction for the charge under s. 302 read with s. 34 is set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether the evidence established the appellant's complicity in the murder to support the charges under Section 302 read with Section 109 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and for conspiracy.

facts.fact: There were constant disputes and strained relations between the appellant (accused no. 4) and the deceased over a right of passage and water, which established animus (motive).
The day before the murder, the appellant exhorted his companions to kill the deceased.
On the day of the murder, the appellant threatened to kill the deceased.
A witness, Jaitunbi (P.W. 5), testified that on the night of the murder, the appellant told his nephew to move from a cot because a dead body was going to be placed there.
Another witness, Laxmibai (P.W. 7), saw the appellant with two other persons following the deceased just 15-20 minutes before the murder occurred.

law.law_text: Section 109 of the IPC (abetment) can be applied even if the abettor is not present when the crime is committed, as long as they instigated the offence or engaged in a conspiracy to commit it.

Criminal conspiracy under Section 120-B is an agreement between two or more people to do an illegal act. Since conspiracies are hatched in secret, they can be proven by circumstantial evidence, including surrounding circumstances and the antecedent and subsequent conduct of the accused.

application.application_text: The Court found that the evidence of the long-standing disputes, combined with the appellant's open threats and exhortations to kill the deceased, fully established both his animus and his role in instigating the murder.

The testimony that the appellant was preparing for a dead body and was seen following the victim shortly before the attack was considered strong circumstantial evidence supporting the charge of a pre-planned criminal conspiracy.

The Court concluded that this collective evidence was sufficient to prove the appellant's involvement, noting that proof of conspiracy is often inferential but must be founded on solid facts, which it found to be present in this case.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the evidence clearly established the appellant's complicity in the murder. The combination of motive (strained relations), direct instigation (threats and exhortations to kill), and circumstantial evidence linking him to the crime immediately before it happened was sufficient to fully support the convictions for abetment of murder under Section 302 read with Section 109 IPC and for criminal conspiracy.

issue.issue_text: Whether the evidence established beyond a reasonable doubt the appellant's presence at or near the spot of the murder to sustain a conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).

facts: A witness, Jaitunbi (P.W. 5), testified that on the night of the murder, the appellant told his nephew to move from a cot because a dead body was to be kept there.
Another witness, Laxmibai (P.W. 7), testified that the appellant and two others followed the deceased about 20 minutes before the murder was reported.
This evidence suggested it was "highly probable" that the appellant was present with the other co-accused or was nearby at the time of the murder.
law: To sustain a conviction, the prosecution must establish the accused's guilt "beyond a reasonable doubt."
A charge under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the IPC requires proof that the accused was present at or near the scene of the crime, participating in furtherance of a common intention.
application: The Court found that while the evidence made the appellant's presence at the scene highly probable, it was not sufficient to meet the standard of proof required for a criminal conviction.
The Court reasoned that the evidence did not eliminate the possibility that the appellant might have stayed away after following the deceased, leaving the other co-accused to commit the murder.
Because this alternative possibility could not be ruled out, the evidence was deemed insufficient to prove the appellant's presence at the spot "beyond a reasonable doubt."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court gave the appellant the benefit of the doubt and set aside his conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the IPC, as the evidence did not establish his presence at or near the scene of the murder beyond a reasonable doubt.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the evidence established the appellant's complicity in the murder to support the charges under Section 302 read with Section 109 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and for conspiracy.
appellant_arguments: The evidence presented did not support the High Court's conclusion that the appellant was complicit in the murder or part of a conspiracy.
respondent_arguments: The evidence established the appellant's complicity, as he was seen following the deceased with two or three persons just before the murder. Furthermore, a witness testified that the appellant told his nephew to move from a cot because a dead body was to be kept there, indicating prior knowledge and planning.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the evidence established beyond a reasonable doubt the appellant's presence at or near the spot of the murder to sustain a conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
appellant_arguments: The evidence was not sufficient to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the appellant was present at the spot when the murder was actually committed. It is possible that after following the deceased, he stayed away while the other co-accused committed the murder.
respondent_arguments: The evidence showing the appellant followed the deceased with others just before the murder made it highly probable that he was present at the scene with the co-accused during the crime, thereby sharing a common intention.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Section 34 embodies the principle of joint liability in the doing of a criminal act, the essence of that liability being the existence of a common intention. Participation in the commission of the offence in furtherance of the common intention invites its application.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The evidence clearly established the appellant's complicity in the murder and supported the charges for abetment (s. 109 IPC) and conspiracy. However, regarding the charge of sharing a common intention at the scene (s. 34 IPC), the court found that while it was highly probable the appellant was present or nearby during the actual murder, the evidence failed to establish this beyond a reasonable doubt. Therefore, the appellant must be given the benefit of the doubt on the charge under s. 302 read with s. 34.
legal_tests_applied: For a conviction under Section 34 IPC, the court applies the principle of joint liability where the essence is the existence of a common intention, and 'Participation in the commission of the offence in furtherance of the common intention invites its application.'
The standard of proof required to establish an accused's presence and participation at the scene of a crime for a conviction under Section 34 is 'beyond reasonable doubt'.

For conspiracy, an inference of 'pre-planning to do away with the deceased' can be 'reasonably be drawn from the circumstances established in the case,' such as the accused following the deceased just before the incident.
why_appellant_lost: The court upheld the conviction for conspiracy and abetment because the evidence showed the appellant 'was seen following the deceased just before the murder with two or three persons.'

The court accepted the lower court's inference that 'all the four accused persons must have hatched a plan to commit the murder of Mohd. Yahya... and it was in pursuance of this conspiracy that Mohd. Yahya was murdered.'

The court found the evidence of key witnesses (Noorjehan P.W. 11 and Jaitunbi P.W. 5) to be credible, noting that although they were 'to a certain extent, interested their evidence appeared to it to be natural and its tenor did not show that they were deposing falsely.'
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully established conspiracy and abetment by presenting evidence that the appellant 'was seen following the deceased just before the murder with two or three persons.'

The respondent convinced the court to draw an inference from the circumstances that 'all the four accused persons must have hatched a plan to commit the murder... and it was in pursuance of this conspiracy that Mohd. Yahya was murdered.'
The respondent's witnesses (Noorjehan P.W. 11 and Jaitunbi P.W. 5) were deemed credible by the court, which found their evidence 'natural' and not false, thereby supporting the charges of complicity.
